newsitem.title: JAPAN: Aid lets N.Korea up zinc exports to Japan--traders.
newsitem.headline: Aid lets N.Korea up zinc exports to Japan--traders.

text.p: Famine-stricken North Korea is boosting zinc exports to Japan as international aid has allowed it to sell more of the metal instead of using it in barter trade for food, traders in Tokyo said on Thursday.

"We heard some 1,500 tonnes of zinc has arrived in western Japan from North Korea over the past two months," said a metal trader at a European house. "We understand they're able to boost exports because they're receiving more and more free grain."
Official statistics show Japanese zinc imports from North Korea totalled 414 tonnes in both June and May, down from 549 tonnes in June last year. No data is yet available for July.

Several zinc traders in Tokyo, including those at Japanese smelters, said they had seen increased zinc sales offers from North Korea recently. They said Pyongyang appeared to have been encouraged by a rally in the metal's price on the world market to more than $1,500 per tonne from just above $1,000 in January.

Only a few months ago North Korean zinc sales offers to Japan dried up as the Stalinist nation was using the metal to barter for food, the traders said. North Korea's zinc production has also fallen sharply in recent years due to shortages of electricity, ore and hard currency.
In June, it failed to honour a metal-for-wheat barter deal with U.S. grain giant Cargill.

Cargill Inc chairman Ernie Micek said in Washington last week that the deal foundered due to the volume of international food aid donated to North Korea, which prompted Pyongyang to start selling its zinc rather than bartering it for food.

Tokyo traders said it was difficult to sell North Korean zinc to end-users, as many had switched to Chinese and Russian metal after Pyongyang's annual output slid below 100,000 tonnes from around 230,000 tonnes five years ago.
"Some trade houses seem to have ended up holding the North Korean zinc because they couldn't sell it to end-users," one zinc trader said. "It's putting pressure on zinc premiums for Japan."
